title: The dose makes the poison, and the L D fifty

segs.text: Section six. Dose and the L D fifty. The dose makes the poison, a saying attributed to Paracelsus, means any substance can harm at a high enough dose. That is why medications are poisons too. The second half of the idea is that the harmful dose differs enormously from one compound to another. Toxicologists compare compounds on that scale with the L D fifty, the lethal dose that kills fifty percent of the animals given the compound. It is not half the lethal dose. The values on her table come from animal exposure studies in rats.

Ethyl alcohol sits at the top of the table, with an L D fifty of ten thousand milligrams per kilogram. Botulinum toxin sits at the bottom, at one hundred-thousandth of a milligram per kilogram. The two differ by a factor of a billion. A smaller L D fifty means a smaller dose kills half the animals, so the compound is more lethal. A higher L D fifty means the compound is less acutely lethal, not more toxic. A large L D fifty is still not the same as safe, because alcohol poisoning still kills at the right dose. She said, So the dose makes the poison, but you have to know what compound you're talking about too.

Botulinum toxin is a toxin in the sense of section one, because a living organism makes it. The botulinum bacteria do not need oxygen, so they can grow sealed inside a can of a low-acid vegetable such as beans, peas or corn; tomatoes are usually fine. As they multiply, they make the toxin and build up pressure, so the can squirts when opened. What kills is the toxin, not the bacteria, and in her words cooking does not break the toxin down. She said, If the can squirts, throw it away, don't cook with it.
